wstep: This card describes NCHFP pickled beets: cooked beets in a vinegar, sugar and water brine, hot packed and processed in a boiling-water bath.

sekcje.naglowek: Why the recipe must not be changed
akapity: Beets are not an acid food: their natural pH is about 5.30–6.60.
Rules in the USA count as acid foods only those with a natural pH of 4.6 or below.
The whole product needs a minimum, uniform level of acid to prevent the growth of botulism bacteria.
Do not change the proportions of vinegar, vegetables and water, and do not use vinegar of unknown acidity; use only recipes with tested proportions.
For pickles, white distilled vinegar and cider vinegar with 5% acidity are recommended.
Penn State Extension advises vinegar of 5–7% acidity for home food preservation and advises against diluting vinegar with water unless a research-tested recipe says so.

JarAtlas rule (cautious, for readers outside the USA): use white distilled (spirit) vinegar or cider vinegar labelled 5% or 6% acidity; do not use 10% vinegar and do not dilute it with water to make 5% vinegar; add only the water the recipe lists.
NCHFP uses US measures: a cup holds about 237 ml.

For about 8 pint jars NCHFP uses 7 pounds (about 3.2 kg) of beets 2 to 2 1/2 inches (about 5–6.4 cm) in diameter, 4 cups of vinegar with 5% acidity, 1 1/2 teaspoons of canning or pickling salt, 2 cups of sugar and 2 cups of water.
Spices: 2 cinnamon sticks and 12 whole cloves; 4 to 6 onions 2 to 2 1/2 inches in diameter are optional.
Trim off the beet tops, leaving 1 inch (about 2.5 cm) of stem and the roots, so the beets do not bleed color.
Wash the beets thoroughly and sort them by size.
Cover beets of similar size with boiling water and cook until tender, about 25–30 minutes.
Caution (NCHFP): drain and discard the cooking liquid; then cool the beets.
Trim off the roots and stems, slip off the skins and cut the beets into slices 1/4 inch (about 0.6 cm) thick.
Peel and thinly slice the onions.
Combine the vinegar, salt, sugar and fresh water.
Put the spices in a cheesecloth bag, add it to the vinegar mixture and bring to a boil.
Add the beets and onions, simmer for 5 minutes and remove the spice bag.
Fill the jars with beets and onions, leaving 1/2 inch (about 1.3 cm) of headspace.
Add the hot vinegar solution, again leaving 1/2 inch of headspace.
Put on the lids and process.
NCHFP also allows whole baby beets 1 to 1 1/2 inches (about 2.5–3.8 cm) in diameter: follow the same directions, but pack them whole without slicing; the onions may be left out.
At 0–1000 ft (up to 300 m) process pint and quart jars in a boiling-water bath for 30 minutes.
Above 1000 ft the food may spoil if the time is not increased.
At 1001–3000 ft (above 300 m up to 900 m) process them for 35 minutes.
At 3001–6000 ft (above 900 m up to 1800 m) process them for 40 minutes.
Above 6000 ft (above 1800 m) process them for 45 minutes.
The card converts feet to metres and rounds the limits down, towards the longer time: 1000 ft becomes 300 m, 3000 ft becomes 900 m and 6000 ft becomes 1800 m.
Shortening the time or cooling jars in cold water can also lead to spoilage.
NCHFP times are for US jar sizes: a pint holds about 473 ml and a quart about 946 ml.
JarAtlas rule (NCHFP does not test metric jars): this recipe has one time for pints and quarts, so it applies to jars of up to 946 ml, for example 0.5 l or 0.9 l.
This NCHFP recipe gives no time for jars larger than a quart, such as 1 l, so JarAtlas recommends smaller jars.
When you take the hot jars out of the canner, do not retighten the lids or bands; this can cut through the gasket and cause seal failures.

Cool the jars at room temperature for 12 to 24 hours, then remove only the screw bands (the metal rings of two-piece lids), leaving the flat lids on the jars, and test the seal: press the middle of the lid, and if it springs up when you release it, the jar is not sealed.

NCHFP calls Mason-type canning jars with self-sealing two-piece lids (a flat lid and a screw band) the best choice, and this seal test and the method on this card assume them; NCHFP does not recommend other commercial jars whose mouths cannot be sealed with two-piece canning lids for canning any food at home.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): use this card only with jars that take two-piece canning lids; it gives no method for twist-off jars or jars with glass lids, so do not use them for this recipe.
A sealed lid is concave, curved down slightly in the centre; if the centre is flat or bulging, the jar may not be sealed.
If a jar has not sealed at this check, keep it in the refrigerator and eat it within several days.

Store sealed jars in a clean, cool, dark, dry place, not above 95 °F (35 °C) and not near hot pipes, a stove or a furnace, in an uninsulated attic or in direct sunlight; in such conditions the food may spoil.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): keep an opened jar in the refrigerator and use it within 1 week.
Before using a stored jar, check that the lid is tight and holds a vacuum: a good seal has a concave centre.
Look for streaks of dried food running from the top of the jar, rising air bubbles and unnatural colour.
When opening the jar, check for an unnatural smell, spurting liquid and cotton-like mould on the food or under the lid.
Do not taste food from a jar with an unsealed lid or with signs of spoilage.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): throw out such a jar.

NCHFP warns that spoiled low-acid foods, including tomatoes, may show different signs of spoilage or very few, so every suspect jar of such food should be treated as if it had produced botulinum toxin and handled carefully.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): handle every suspect jar from this card this way, because its main ingredient is low in acid or close to the acidity limit.
If a suspect jar is still sealed, put it in a heavy garbage bag, close the bag and put it in a regular trash container.

If it is unsealed, open or leaking, NCHFP says it should be detoxified before disposal; JarAtlas does not repeat that procedure here, so follow the detoxification and clean-up steps on the NCHFP page “Identifying and Handling Spoiled Canned Food” (nchfp.uga.edu/how/can/general-information/identifying-and-handling-spoiled-canned-food/) and avoid contact with suspect food or liquid.
Contact with botulinum toxin can be fatal if it is swallowed or enters through any openings in the skin, so wear rubber or heavy plastic gloves when handling suspect jars and cleaning up.
